prompt.context: Our client is A+Airline Co., the third largest airline in the United States by passengers carried. This week, we have been flying on our primary competitor, Gamma Airline, and we noticed something interesting: they stopped accepting cash for in-flight food and beverage services and they now only accept major credit cards.
prompt.question: The CEO of A+Airline Co. wants to know: why did Gamma Airline switch from a Cash & Card system to a credit card only system, and should we follow them?

clarifying_info.q: Do all passengers on the airplane have a credit card?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. Roughly 99% of all consumers purchase their airline tickets using a credit card, so all consumers on an airplane have a credit card available to them.

clarifying_info.q: What items does A+Airline sell on flights?
clarifying_info.a: Only food and alcoholic beverage items are sold on A+Airline flights.

clarifying_info.q: Is this decision for domestic or international flights?
clarifying_info.a: This is a US Domestic decision only. Ignore international.

clarifying_info.q: Has any other airline made this switch?
clarifying_info.a: Gamma is the only airline that has made the switch; however all other airlines are evaluating the switch.

clarifying_info.q: How similar is A+Airline to Gamma?
clarifying_info.a: For the purposes of this case, Gamma and A+Airline should be considered to be exactly the same in all regards.

exhibits.title: An Average A+Airline Flight
exhibits.shows: Seat and passenger breakdown for a Boeing 737-800: total seats (200), class breakdown (First Class 25%, Economy 75%), load factors, business/leisure mix, purchase rates by traveler type, average spend per purchaser, and current cash vs. card payment split.

data.note: First Class Passengers Receive Free Food & Beverage

exhibits.title: A+Airline Cash & Card Operations
exhibits.shows: Two parallel process flows side by side: the current Cash Management Process (8 steps, 31 days total time from flight to bank deposit, 2% fee on all cash collected, requires 5 Cash Handlers per airport and 2 employees in an onsite Cash Processing Center) and the Credit Card Process (3 steps, 24 hours total time, 2% fee on all transactions).

framework: Revenue Changes: Loss of Cash-Only customers who will not convert to card vs. potential increase in card-paying customers
Cost Changes: Benefit of eliminating Cash Management overhead costs vs. incremental credit card processing fee (note: both systems have same 2% fee, so fee impact is a wash)
Cash Flow / TVM Changes: Impact of receiving payment 30 days sooner (interest, early supplier payment, paying down credit lines) and working capital freed by eliminating $50 in change per flight

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the total market size in dollars for food and beverage purchases on an average flight, and determine the current split between cash and card purchases.
questions.guidance: Interviewee should work through: (1) Economy occupants = 150 seats x 80% = 120. Split 50/50 into 60 Business, 60 Leisure. (2) First Class = 50 seats x 100% = 50 occupants, all Business, but they get free food so they do NOT purchase. (3) Purchasers among Economy: Business 60 x 75% = 45 purchasing at $10 = $450; Leisure 60 x 25% = 15 purchasing at $5 = $75. Total purchasers = 60, total spend = $525. (4) Cash portion = 20% x $525 = $105; Card portion = 80% x $525 = $420.

math.setup: Economy seats = 150 x 80% load = 120 occupants. 50% business = 60 business economy passengers; 50% leisure = 60 leisure economy passengers. First Class = 50 x 100% = 50 passengers, all business, but free food so no purchases. Business purchasers: 60 x 75% = 45, avg $10 each. Leisure purchasers: 60 x 25% = 15, avg $5 each.
math.answer: Total market = $525 per flight. Current cash spend = $105, card spend = $420.

questions.prompt: Of the current cash customers, we will lose 1/3 who refuse to switch to card. Calculate the revenue loss per flight.
questions.guidance: Interviewee must not round. Cash spend is $105. Cash purchasers = 20 total (20% of 60 purchasers). Split by type: Business cash = 20% x 45 = 9; Leisure cash = 20% x 15 = 3. Lose 1/3: lose 3 Business ($30) and 1 Leisure ($5). Total revenue loss = $35 per flight.

math.setup: Total cash purchasers: 20% x 60 = 12 purchasers (alternatively computed by value: $105 in cash revenue). Business cash customers = 20% x 45 = 9; Leisure cash customers = 20% x 15 = 3. Lose 1/3 of each group.
steps: Lose 1/3 of 9 business cash customers = 3 customers lost
Lose 1/3 of 3 leisure cash customers = 1 customer lost
math.answer: Revenue loss = $35 per flight (3 business customers at $10 + 1 leisure customer at $5).

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what are the cost implications of switching from Cash & Card to Card Only?
questions.guidance: The interviewee should notice: (1) Both cash and card processes have a 2% fee on collections, so switching does not change the fee burden — it is a wash. (2) The cash process requires 5 Cash Handlers + 2 Cash Processing Center employees = 7 total employees per airport — these could be eliminated. When asked, the interviewer confirms the per-flight overhead saving from eliminating cash management is $35/flight. Net cost impact = save $35 per flight.

math.setup: Cash fee = 2% on cash collected. Card fee = 2% on card collected. After switch, all revenue is card — same 2% fee. Overhead saving from eliminating 7 employees per airport = $35 per flight (given).
steps: Fee delta: 2% cash (eliminated) - 2% card (on all revenue) = wash (0 net change in fee)
Overhead saving: $35 per flight (elimination of cash management staff)
math.answer: Net cost saving = $35 per flight. The 2% processing fee is neutral; the saving comes entirely from eliminating cash management overhead.

questions.prompt: Qualitatively explain the impact of receiving payment 30 days sooner (credit card process takes 24 hours vs. cash process takes 31 days).
questions.guidance: Strong answers will mention: (1) Time Value of Money — money received sooner can be invested in interest-earning accounts or growth projects; (2) Early supplier payments — A+Airline can pay suppliers early and capture discounts; (3) Faster debt repayment — can pay down lines of credit sooner, reducing interest expense; (4) Working Capital — eliminating $50 in change loaded per flight frees up working capital and reduces losses from theft and cash damage.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the quantitative analysis, what additional qualitative factors should A+Airline consider when making this decision?

categories.name: Revenue Upside
ideas: Faster card transactions reduce wait time per passenger, increasing probability that economy passengers at the back complete a purchase before the service cart passes
Consumers who pay by card tend to spend more than cash payers — removing the cash option may lift average transaction value
Speed improvement may allow flight attendants to serve more passengers per flight

categories.name: Cash Flow & Working Capital
ideas: Receiving payment in 24 hours vs. 31 days significantly accelerates cash inflows
$50 in change loaded per flight can be redeployed productively across the entire fleet
Reduced risk of cash theft by employees or passengers
Reduced risk of counterfeit currency losses

categories.name: Operational Simplification
ideas: Eliminates 7 employees per airport (5 cash handlers + 2 processing center staff)
Simplifies end-of-flight reconciliation for flight attendants
Reduces training burden for new flight attendants

categories.name: Competitive & Strategic
ideas: Gamma Airline has already switched — a signal the economics work
All other airlines are evaluating the switch, suggesting this is an industry trend
Being an early mover after Gamma may provide learning advantages
Consistent with broader industry move toward cashless transactions

categories.name: Risks & Downsides
ideas: Small segment of cash-only travelers will be permanently lost
Potential negative PR from passengers who prefer cash
Technology dependency — wireless terminals must function reliably on every flight
Potential regulatory scrutiny in jurisdictions requiring cash acceptance

recommendation: A+Airline should switch to a credit card only system for in-flight food and beverage purchases

On a per-flight basis, the revenue loss of $35 (4 lost customers) is exactly offset by the $35 overhead cost saving from eliminating cash management — but the saving flows to the bottom line while the revenue loss is top-line, making the net profit impact positive
Additional qualitative benefits — faster collections, improved working capital, simplified operations, and likely higher per-transaction spend — further support the switch
risks: Loss of a small number of cash-only customers who will not convert (estimated 4 per flight)
Technology risk if card terminals malfunction on a flight
Potential negative customer perception or PR backlash from a small minority of passengers
next_steps: Confirm terminal reliability and have a backup process for technology failures
Communicate the change to customers clearly in advance to manage expectations
Monitor actual revenue and customer satisfaction data in the first months post-switch to validate the model
Evaluate whether the freed cash management staff can be redeployed elsewhere or whether headcount reduction creates additional savings
